Gig
GIG
noun (Silent Generation slang)
Of uncertain origin. Jazz musicians used gig for a paid engagement, especially a single night’s job, from the 1920s; by the 1940s and 1950s every working musician lived on gigs, and later any job at all could be a gig. The older English gig — a whirling toy, a light two-wheeled carriage, a ship’s boat — is the word Webster recorded in 1828; no link between it and the musicians’ sense is proven.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

To a dance-band trumpeter in 1948, a gig was a job — Saturday night at the Elks hall, twelve dollars and supper. Musicians lived gig to gig. The word has spread, and your generation uses it for any job, especially a short one. The Bible honours the working musician. Young David’s first job at the palace was a gig of sorts: when Saul was troubled, "David took an harp, and played with his hand: so Saul was refreshed, and was well" (1Sa 16:23). The psalm says to "play skilfully with a loud noise" (Psa 33:3) — skill is a way of honouring God. And the musician deserves his pay like any worker: "the labourer is worthy of his hire" (Luk 10:7). The danger in a gig is the attitude that can come with it — it is only a gig, only for tonight, not worth my best. Scripture shuts that door: "whatsoever ye do, do it heartily, as to the Lord, and not unto men" (Col 3:23), and "Whatsoever thy hand findeth to do, do it with thy might" (Ecc 9:10). A Christian plays the Elks hall as if the Lord were in the front row, because He is. And the best news for a man living gig to gig is that his life is not a string of gigs. In Christ he has a calling, a Master who never lays him off, and a reward that does not run out.

Webster 1828 Definition

Silent Generation slang (jazz from the 1920s; common 1940s–50s) for a musician’s paid engagement, later any job — work Scripture honours when it is done heartily, as to the Lord (Col 3:23), with the labourer worthy of his hire.

GIG, n. (Silent Generation slang, 1940s–50s; jazz musicians’ word from the 1920s) A paid engagement for a musician, especially one night’s job; later, any job. "We’ve got a gig at the Legion hall Saturday."

Webster (1828) — GIG, noun 1. Any little thing that is whirled round in play. 2. A light carriage with one pair of wheels, drawn by one horse; a chair or chaise. 3. A fiddle.

Decode for families: a gig is a job, often a short one — but a Christian works every one of them for the Lord.

Key Scripture

1Sa 16:23 — "And it came to pass, when the evil spirit from God was upon Saul, that David took an harp, and played with his hand: so Saul was refreshed, and was well, and the evil spirit departed from him."

Psa 33:3 — "Sing unto him a new song; play skilfully with a loud noise."

Luk 10:7 — "And in the same house remain, eating and drinking such things as they give: for the labourer is worthy of his hire. Go not from house to house."

Col 3:23 — "And whatsoever ye do, do it heartily, as to the Lord, and not unto men;"

Ecc 9:10 — "Whatsoever thy hand findeth to do, do it with thy might; for there is no work, nor device, nor knowledge, nor wisdom, in the grave, whither thou goest."

Modern Corruption

An honest working word; the only snare is the half-hearted attitude that treats a short job as not worth one’s best, which Scripture answers with work done heartily as to the Lord.

expand to see more

Gig is a plain word for honest work, and nothing in it needs correcting. Musicians who played weddings, dances, and church suppers through the 1940s and 1950s were laborers worthy of their hire (Luk 10:7), and many of them were faithful men.

The word can carry an attitude, though: a gig is temporary, so why give it everything? Scripture answers that every job, long or short, is done before the Lord (Col 3:23; Ecc 9:10). There are no small gigs when the Master is watching.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

English gig (whirling toy; light carriage; ship’s boat, by 1828) — separate, uncertain → 1920s jazz gig (a paid engagement) → 1940s–50s working musicians’ word → any job.

expand to see more

Middle English gigge — a whirling thing; origin uncertain

1828 Webster: gig — a top; a light carriage; a ship’s boat

1920s jazz: gig — a paid engagement, one night’s job

1940s–50s: the working musician’s everyday word

Later: gig — any job, especially a short one

Usage
